chapter_theme: The second half of Malaipadukadam takes the bards from the patron's mountain, whose countless sounds make the 'resonance of the mountain', down its dangerous roads and through the hospitality of herders, bowmen, farmers and fishers to Nannan's town and court, where his welcome, his reflection that only fame outlives death, and his gifts close the poem on his title.
structure_note: The chapter is one continuous instruction: a list of sounds closing on மலைபடு கடாஅம் (348), the road with its hazards and hosts, each stage ending in கழிமின் (go on) or பெறுகுவிர் (you will get), then the town, the court, and the parting. Every core unit except 352-372, 373-389 and 390-402 was moved to a sentence or item break, giving 18 units.

pattupattu:10:308-322.reading: The catalogue of the hill's sounds goes on: the thunderous roar that the herd sends echoing along the high slope when a bright, strong tiger springs; the endless wailing of a troop of leaf-eating monkeys crowding round when a black-fingered mother loses her grip and her untaught young falls into a deep cleft; the glee of the forest men who, by a ladder fixed up a cliff no stag can climb, have taken a great haul of honey and, having broken a hard stronghold, say it will serve as guest-tribute for their lord of the shapely spear; and the kuravai the hill men dance with their women on the sky-touching heights after a day of brewing toddy, to the beat of the small deer-skin drum.
pattupattu:10:308-322.nuance: Line 308 closes a clause begun in the previous chapter (a mate who guards, the limit of strength). Every item here is a noun of sound (தழங்குகுரல், பூசல், உவகை's shout, குரவை), all of them subjects waiting for the verb இயம்ப in line 348: the idyll's title, the 'resonance born of the mountain', is this whole inventory. The forest men's honey and fort-spoil are reserved as tribute for the lord before they are enjoyed.
pattupattu:10:308-322.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 308-321: line 322 (வான்றோய் மீமிசை அயருங் குரவை) completes the item of the kuravai begun in lines 320 and 321, and line 323 opens the item of the echoing stream.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill's life is described as the wealth and joy of the patron's land, whose people bring him tribute: praise of the patron (porul 2.27)

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the herd at the tiger's leap

pattupattu:10:323-339.reading: More sounds: the deep echo in the clefts where the rocky stream roars as if a tall fine chariot were coming along the track; the cries of mahouts speaking a mixed tongue to cool the rage of a fierce elephant caught in a deep pool, so as to tie it to a great post; the shouts of girls scaring parrots from every millet plot, beating split-bamboo clappers; the clamour as a fine bull with shaking hump, strayed from its herd, clashes with unfailing strength against the eager bull of the wild cattle come down the hill, while cowherds and hill men cheer together and the kulavi and kurinji are crushed; and the noise of the boys who, brandishing fragrant kaanthal stalks, drive off the calves to get the seeds from the leftovers of the sweet jackfruit segments they have eaten.
pattupattu:10:323-339.nuance: The mahouts' விரவுமொழி, a speech of mixed words, is one of the few signs in the idyll of the many tongues of the hill country. The bull fight brings together the herders of the slopes (கோவலர்) and the hill men (குறவர்) in one cheer: the patron's land is shown as a meeting of peoples.
pattupattu:10:323-339.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 322-340: it begins after குரவை (322) and ends at the item of the boys, closed by ஓதை in line 339; line 340 opens the item of the sugar mills.

thinai_evidence.note: the work and play of the patron's hill people, heard as one resonance in his praise

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the rocky stream echoing in the clefts

pattupattu:10:340-351.reading: And the work-song of the sugar cane that suddenly bursts its joints in every mill, the vallai song of the girls pounding millet, the drums and the hill echoes of those who guard the taro and turmeric from boars: all these together, gathered in the hollows and on the heights, past counting, make the resonance of the mountain sound in every direction; his wide hill, where the women wear garlands of coloured flowers and the drum never sleeps in the broad town, is like a festival.
pattupattu:10:340-351.nuance: Line 348 is the line that names the poem: மலைபடு கடாஅம், the resonance born of the mountain, compared by its very word (கடாம், the musth of an elephant) to a living beast. The whole list from the previous chapter to here is the subject of இயம்ப. The vehicle of line 340 is uncertain: the mills may be likened to rain clouds for their noise or for the steam over them.
pattupattu:10:340-351.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 341-351: it begins at line 340, the start of the item of the sugar mills (ஆலைதொறு ... ஏத்தமும், 340 to 341).

thinai_evidence.note: the sum of the hill's sounds is named as the glory of the patron's mountain

comparisons.tenor: the sugar mills, roaring as when rain clouds gather

pattupattu:10:352-372.reading: Having looked and listened till your eyes are cooled, and praised the many things sweet to eat, saying 'there is more to come for us', you who keep the old custom should leave behind the great thundering mountain of the lord whose fortunate chest loves battle, let your viraliyar sing kurinji on the fragrant rainy slope, worship it with joined hands and go on; when the flock of rain clouds, so low on the dark hill that a hand could touch it, sprays its fine drizzle, enter clefts like wells so that your kin, who cannot tell the way, keep the instruments they carry from harm; and in the gorge where boulders roll and even to stand and look makes the eyes swim, keep away from the broken cliff, use the head-stick of your earth-smeared drum as a staff, guard against slipping and lean on it as you go, for the dangers are very many.
pattupattu:10:352-372.nuance: Leaving the mountain is itself a rite: the troupe sings the mountain's own mode, kurinji, and bows to it before going. The care in the instructions is for the instruments as much as for the people: the drum's stick becomes a walking staff, so the bard's craft is what carries him through the danger.

thinai_evidence.note: the guide's instructions for the road to the patron: the ஆற்றுப்படை speech itself

comparisons.tenor: the rain clouds lying low on the hill
the fine drizzle the clouds spray
the deep clefts that serve as shelter

pattupattu:10:373-389.reading: Over the path where rocks sharp as heated spearheads are guarded by the sun, travel only when the rays' heat has eased; his land has strongholds that shake kings from their footing, with his retinue that never leaves him, whose fame has spread, and many shields raised high like clouds; at every opening of the thickets tangled like braids, keep from the swift-springing shaft the man ahead has drawn, guard the bowl of your sweet yaazh and the stretched head of your drum, keep your grip, and go slowly; boulders packed together like fighting elephants stand in the dripping forest beyond counting, and at the forks of the path there are countless stones planted with the names of undying fame of the honourable warriors who gave themselves on the good path when the hostile foe was routed with a shout.
pattupattu:10:373-389.nuance: The shaft of line 380 is most naturally the branch the walker in front has bent aside, which springs back like an arrow; the reading is not certain. The hero-stones do not mark danger, as they do on the akam roads: they carry names (பெயரொடு நட்ட), and the guide counts them as part of the land's glory. Hour is a precaution: cross the hot rock only when the sun has weakened.

thinai_evidence.note: the road's hazards and the patron's strongholds and warrior stones, told as his land's might

comparisons.tenor: the sharp rock of the path

pattupattu:10:390-402.reading: As your songs please, keep the ancient custom, lower the neck of your instrument and hurry on; you newcomers who have never known this land should tie knots of grass where the ways cross, so as to know the names of the places you are bound for; there are many forks of the forest path where the god stands high in the kadamba with a fine trunk on which letters have been scratched with stones, and many wastes that the foes who fled without joining battle tremble even to mention; if you say you are going to the generous lord with the honey-dripping garland, whose hand flings away chariots and who does not hoard, his ancient town of old lineage is that way, so it is for people like us.
pattupattu:10:390-402.nuance: The tree with letters scratched on it (கல்லெறிந் தெழுதிய, 395) is a signpost: writing on the road, an early witness to letters used for travellers. Lines 391 (மருப்பிகுத்து) and 401 to 402 are hard: what is lowered may be the horn-neck of the yaazh, and தொஃறிணை and ஆங்கனம் அற்றே are read here as 'of old lineage' and 'it is that way', which I cannot confirm.

thinai_evidence.note: directions to the patron whose generosity is the goal of the road

pattupattu:10:403-417.reading: Rest where you tire and go on without fear: beyond the forest where the stag stands calling, remembering the beloved doe the tiger came for, and past the mullai country of fragrant creepers where the red-eyed bull of the wild cattle, frightened by the sound of bows, rushes into the thicket, the cowherds of the hedged land, whose herds with their bulls have gone to other pastures, will pour out the sweet milk of their white cows to the joy of the bangled women, and the loneliness of leaving home in hope of gain will go far from you, and you will be like new; if you come in at nightfall, where the many flocks of rams, ewes and white goats, mixed like the rows of grain at a barter, bleat like the sea in the noisy waste, you will get milk and porridge without asking.
pattupattu:10:403-417.nuance: The stag calling for the doe the tiger took is an image akam poets use for loss, but here it is only the edge of a forest the troupe passes on its way to milk and porridge; in a puram guide poem it carries no hidden sense. The bards' homesickness (புலம்பு) is cured by food, not by return.
pattupattu:10:403-417.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 403-416: the condition of line 416 (எல்லினிர் புகினே) is completed by பெறுகுவிர் in line 417, which ends the sentence.

thinai_evidence.note: the hospitality of the herders in the patron's land, promised to the bard

comparisons.tenor: the mixed flocks of rams, ewes and white goats

pattupattu:10:418-427.reading: Sleep on beds of trampled hide flayed from beasts, soft as a mattress packed with fine hair, with the fire for company, and go on; if you meet a band of curved-bow Kooliyar, whose sharp arrows outrun a shout, and say you are going to the husband of the creeper-slender lady, whose unbowing manhood wore down those who stood against him, they will gather meat and roots and bring them to you: there they are guardians, not attackers; go your way, for that is their nature.
pattupattu:10:418-427.nuance: The patron is named only through his wife (கொடியோள் கணவன்) and his manhood, yet saying it is a safe-conduct: men whose arrows are faster than a call for help become providers. The fear the bowmen would raise is called up only to be cancelled (உடற்றுநர் இல்லை), so no meyppadu is shown.
pattupattu:10:418-427.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 417-427: line 417 moved to the previous unit, which it completes; this unit begins at துய்ம்மயிர் (418).

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's name turns the road's bowmen into hosts: praise of his power

pattupattu:10:428-443.reading: Wearing lovely garlands of the soft honey-blooming kadamba clusters and all the bright sprouts the elephant has broken, woven with young leaves and tied with dried fibre, eat, bathe and take what you want on the path through the broken gravel that is cool there, and go on; in every grass-roofed hut built with crowded poles in the wide hollow, so that the toil of your night's labour ends, you will get porridge of bamboo rice red as vengai flowers, and green pulse of avarai with paddy grown on the ridge; and if you rest and stay you will get every day rice fine as beaten gold, cooked in white dense balls with cool fine ghee inside.
pattupattu:10:428-443.nuance: The garland of line 430 is made from what an elephant has left (உம்பல் அகைத்த): the troupe adorns itself with the forest's leftovers. The meals rise in richness as the stay lengthens, from roadside eating to porridge in every hut to ghee-filled rice every day.
pattupattu:10:428-443.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 428-444: line 444 opens the simile (விசையங் கொழித்த பூழி யன்ன) that governs the flour of line 445, so it moves to the next unit; this one ends at பெறுகுவிர், 443.

thinai_evidence.note: the food and rest promised in the patron's hill country

pattupattu:10:444-453.reading: Lighting a blaze of light wood, eat the fine millet flour, like dust sifted from sugar, that holds back other eaters, sleep sweetly together far from the cold, and at dawn take the birds' omens and go on; whether you stay many days or rest and go, his cool fertile country has much good, with groves and lodges, varied as the modes changed on a fine yaazh, in every town on the soft low ground beside sluices struck by water where the thin-trunked kaanji grows.
pattupattu:10:444-453.nuance: The simile of line 451 is a musician's: passing from town to town is like a bard changing the mode on his yaazh, so the landscape is heard as a performance. Line 445's உண்ணுநர்த் தடுத்த is read as a flour so filling or so sweet that it stops the eaters; the sense is not certain. The country now leaves the hills for the watered low ground.
pattupattu:10:444-453.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 428-444 and 445-460: it begins at line 444, whose simile governs the flour of 445, and ends at நாடே, 453, which closes the sentence on his country; line 454 begins the scene of the fields.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's country is praised for its goodness to travellers

comparisons.tenor: the groves and lodges of every town, each different and pleasing

pattupattu:10:454-464.reading: In the fields fragrant with kanpu reeds, the women of the Pazhaiyar, wearing pakandrai garlands, set on the raised bank of a crab-haunted plot the dark-backed vaalai the net-men bring and the red-eyed varaal, like an elephant cow's trunk, taken on the long lines of men who stand to fish, mixed with cut pieces round as the heads of hand drums; and when the workers who make the land rich have finished threshing the hill-like stacks and give out their food, you will get at every threshing floor, in the young sun of morning, toddy from fresh packets poured out of swaying jars.
pattupattu:10:454-464.nuance: Line 460 is a repaired reading (தராய், a raised bank). The workers' gift is made at the moment of harvest: the bard arrives when the land is richest and is fed from the threshing floor itself.
pattupattu:10:454-464.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 445-460 and 461-481: it begins at கண்புமலி (454), where the scene of the fields opens, and ends at பெறுகுவிர், 464.

thinai_evidence.note: the farmers' bounty in the patron's fields, promised to the bard

pattupattu:10:465-477.reading: Eat with your troupe, to the wonder of all who see, white rice cooked with cucumber whose spines are scraped off, food you will say is fit even for Nannan of the strong chariot whose honey-dripping garland is fragrant with bees; then rest, playing marutham on your fine yaazh to the shouts of the field-hands driving their oxen, and go on; watching for the charge of the lone bull buffalo, strayed from its red-eyed herd in fright at the drums of the reapers of white paddy, take the one rich bank of the Seyaru, pleasant to the eye and longed for by those who see it, whose swift head-current roars without pause where bubbles whirl like a potter's wheel, and go on.
pattupattu:10:465-477.nuance: As the troupe played kurinji when leaving the hill (359), here it plays marutham among the fields: the bards change mode with the land. வெள்ளரி may be white grain rather than cucumber; the scraped spines (முள்ளரித்து) favour the cucumber.
pattupattu:10:465-477.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 461-481: it begins at முள்ளரித் (465) and ends at கழிமின், 477; line 478 begins the description of the patron's town.

thinai_evidence.note: the food fit for the patron himself is given to the bard: praise of his land's bounty

comparisons.tenor: the bubbles whirling in the river's current

pattupattu:10:478-491.reading: His ancient town of old valour is not far: within its high rising enclosure where wealth lies asleep, old families who never leave their place live together; its great market is too crowded for its wide space, its ways lie spread like a river, its festival is like a battle, its lanes forking so that scorners fear them; with a din like the sea and like thunder, mansions rising like mountains and like clouds, people dwelling sweetly in a love that knows no quarrel, and cool groves loud with bees; enter without doubting the closely guarded gate whose doors bear the black-butted spears leaned there by bright-sworded warriors who cut off the heads of hostile foes so that kites gather.
pattupattu:10:478-491.nuance: The town is built of two opposites held together: a market crowded like a battle and people living in love without quarrel; the gate is armed against foes and open to bards (அயிராது புகுமின்). Line 481's செருவிற் சாறென ('a festival like a battle') is odd after யாறெனக் கிடந்த, which would suit தெருவின் (streets).
pattupattu:10:478-491.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 461-481 and 482-497: it begins at நிதியந் (478), where the town's description opens, and ends at புகுமின், 491.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron's town and fortress, which the bard may enter freely

pattupattu:10:492-513.reading: In the common ground the suppliants from far lands staying there, remembering the great valour of the red lord who wins his wars, will say 'surely those who have come deserve pity'; all who see you look on you sweetly and gladly, and each comes to meet you with a guest's welcome, so that the toil the long road has beaten into you may end; and there crowd the gifts of the hill: the calf of the gentle-gaited forest cow caught when its herd fled the kadamba whose flowered boughs seem to spit fire, the curve-pawed cub of the silent bear, the great strong-headed ram of the cliff-dwelling varudai with crooked legs and leaping gait, the small-eyed creature that kills the snakes in their holes, the big-eared calf of the soft-eyed wild cow seized by the tiger that lurks in its den, the crooked-legged male monitor that crawls on gravel by ground red as spread lac, the soft-eyed peacock that goes gracing the hill, the forest cock with its forked call, the great drum-like fruits of the forest jack, and the sweet ripe fruit of the fragrant mango, full of juice.
pattupattu:10:492-513.nuance: The welcome is a look before it is a gift: the whole town 'looks sweetly' (அமர்ந்தினிது நோக்கி) on the newcomers. The gifts are the hill's own wild young, caught alive, and its fruits: the patron gives his land, not only his treasury. சேஎய் (493) calls the patron by Murugan's epithet, the red one. தீர்வை (504) is a creature I cannot identify, and the simile of 512 (இடிக்கலப்பு) is unclear.
pattupattu:10:492-513.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 482-497 and 498-513: it begins at மன்றில் (492), where the arrival in the town opens; it ends at line 513 inside the long list of gifts (498 to 531), cut there to keep the units within 30 lines.

thinai_evidence.note: the welcome and gifts awaiting the bard at the patron's town

comparisons.tenor: the flowering boughs of the kadamba

pattupattu:10:514-531.reading: With them the growing creeper whose buds have shot up in the spray, the yam like a yoke carried slung from a pole, the many-faceted fine gems shed from great crystal, the pearl-holding tusks, massive and strong, of an elephant wounded in a fight with a striped tiger, kaanthal with large petals like broken conch bangles, naagam, tilakam and the fragrant heartwood of sandal, green pepper in clusters from the dark pepper vine, well-matured toddy of honey, sweet curd of the forest buffalo poured into bamboo, the ghee-eyed honeycomb that rolls like a wheel down the high slope when the dark-blue ori leaps on it, and wild jack clasped together: all of these, crowding at the long gate of his unbearable war like the broad Kaveri, born on Kudamalai, at the mouth where it plunges into the sea; approach the courtyard thick with the pollen-strewn dung of his elephants, as many as the sky.
pattupattu:10:514-531.nuance: The great simile turns the list into a river: the wealth of the hills flows down to the patron's gate as the Kaveri flows down from Kudamalai to the sea, so the gate is the estuary of the land. What ஓரி (524) names is uncertain.
pattupattu:10:514-531.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 514-528 and 529-543: it ends at முன்னி (531), where the list of gifts and the approach to the courtyard close; line 532 begins the music at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill's riches crowd the patron's gate as tribute: praise of his wealth

comparisons.tenor: the gifts crowding at the patron's gate
the multitude of the patron's elephants

pattupattu:10:532-546.reading: As the drumheads boom as if answering the rain clouds and the holes of the bamboo pipe hum, the sweet-voiced viraliyar, playing marutham on the black-necked small yaazh with strings in unison that never overstep, knowing what is due and keeping their nature by the old custom, first praise the god of great power, then finish the song of welcome, and with long words hail him: 'Lord, scion of those whose good fame does not fail, you who, now that the great ones who could tell merit have died, have paid the debt of giving so that fame does not leave the world today but stays with it'; praising his victories, his many fames and his strength; but he does not let them even tell of their journey: 'Desire brought you; your coming is enough; your toil was great.'
pattupattu:10:532-546.nuance: Giving is called a debt (கொடைக்கடன்), owed to the world now that the old discerning patrons are gone: the patron inherits the obligation along with the line. His interruption is the best praise in the poem: the suppliants are spared the telling of their hardship.
pattupattu:10:532-546.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 529-543 and 544-556: it begins at மழையெதிர் (532), the music in the court, and ends at பெரிதென (546), where the patron's words of welcome close.

thinai_evidence.note: the bards' praise of the patron's giving and fame, and his welcome: paadaan proper

pattupattu:10:547-566.reading: He reflects that those who shone among warriors ready for battle, who, wishing to approach the courtyard of a fortunate city, kept their noisy kin about them on the right, who sat on high thrones among fearless kin with wide inheritance and keen wit, and yet spread their hands saying 'we have nothing', died taking their names with them, and they outnumber the sands of the scarred banks of the Seyaru, whose fierce muddy flood pours down from the high hill's waterfall; 'therefore let our allotted days pass with fame': with that sky-touching heart that gives room to all, gladder than you who came in longing, he looks on you sweetly, wraps your waist with fine cloth whose threads cannot be seen, and feeds you with the fresh fat meat the hounds bring and unfailing rice of long white paddy, welcoming you as on the first day however many days you stay.
pattupattu:10:547-566.nuance: On the reading taken here, இலமென மலர்ந்த கையர் (552) are men who spread empty hands saying 'we have nothing', so their names died with them; read instead as hands that opened when suppliants said 'we have nothing', the lines would say that even great givers died, and fame alone remains. Either way the patron's giving is argued from death. Who speaks lines 547 to 557 is not marked: the patron's thought is given as a quotation closed by என (557).
pattupattu:10:547-566.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 544-556 and 557-572: it begins at பொருமுரண் (547), the reflection on the dead, and ends at பெறுகுவிர் (566), which closes the promise of daily hospitality.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit turns on the thought of death and the fame that outlasts it (perunilai of kaanchi), which becomes the motive for giving

comparisons.tenor: those who died taking their names with them

pattupattu:10:567-583.reading: If you tell him gently, 'we will not stay; we go back to our old village', he will crown the leader among you with a lotus and have the viraliyar wear bright jewels of great worth, and with tall chariots that run in rows like flowing water, hill-like elephants too great to be held, great herds with bulls and ringing bells, cut-maned horses bright in golden trappings and treasure heaped till it wears down the ground, all of it filling the outstretched hands of needy poets, from his great hand with its sliding bracelet that tips as it pours out vessels, never knowing a failure of wealth and rich in kind speech, giving like the rain that suddenly pours on the high peak of Naviram where the bamboo grows, he sends you off with gifts on the first day you ask: he, the lord of the land of hill-ringed dwellings where the mountain waters show like victory flags.
pattupattu:10:567-583.nuance: The whole idyll is one sentence whose subject arrives only in its last word, நாடுகிழவோனே: everything the guide has said waits on the patron's title. The leaving gift is given on the first day it is asked (தலைநாள்), matching the welcome 'as on the first day' (565): neither the welcome nor the farewell wears out.
pattupattu:10:567-583.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 557-572 and 573-583: it begins at செல்வேந் (567), the guests' word of leaving, and runs to the end of the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the parting gifts and the naming of the patron that closes the guide poem

comparisons.tenor: the mountain waters falling from the hills

links.note: Perunthalai Sathanar says the wealthy who gave nothing to the needy are not remembered, while those who set up fame are; in the idyll the patron counts the enthroned rich whose names died with them as more than river sand and decides that his days shall pass with fame.
links.teaches: The argument a bard uses in Purananuru 165 to shame and urge patrons appears in the idyll as the patron's own reasoning, so the guide poem shows the bards' doctrine of fame taken in by the giver as his motive for giving.

links.note: The Kural says nothing stands undying in the world but towering fame; the idyll sets beside the patron's choice of fame a crowd of dead rich men past counting whose names went with them.
links.teaches: The Kural states that fame alone survives without saying what the alternative looks like; the idyll supplies it as a number, the sands of a riverbank, so the couplet's single survivor is measured against a vast forgetting.

links.note: The Kural says giving without the misery of saying 'I have nothing' is found only in the well-born; the patron, hailed as the scion of an unfailing line, will not let the bards even finish telling of their journey before he welcomes them.
links.teaches: One of the senses of the couplet, giving before the asker must speak of his need, is in the idyll a court scene in which the patron cuts short the suppliants' account, and the idyll ties it, as the Kural does, to the giver's lineage.

links.note: The Kural says a guest wilts when the host's face changes; in the idyll everyone in the patron's town looks on the arriving bards sweetly and gladly before any gift is given.
links.teaches: The Kural makes the host's face the guest's first need inside one household; the idyll extends that glad look to a whole town, so the welcoming face becomes a public mark of the patron's realm rather than a private courtesy.

links.note: The guide tells the bards to enter Nannan's heavily guarded gate without hesitation; Purananuru 151 tells a kinsman of Nannan of the golden chariot that the poet's people have shunned his hill because of a door shut against singers.
links.teaches: If both poems speak of one house, the open guarded gate the idyll promises is the standard by which Perunthalai Sathanar shames the kinsman: a lineage's fame for an open door becomes a claim its heirs can fail.

links.note: In the idyll the forest men who have broken a hard stronghold (அருங்குறும் பெறிந்த) set aside their spoil as guest-tribute for their lord; in Akananuru 349 Nannan pours out unasked to weary bards the great wealth taken from broken strongholds (அருங்குறும்பு எறிந்த).
links.teaches: Read together the two poems show a chain of wealth: the spoil of forts taken by the hill people goes to Nannan as tribute and goes out again from him to the bards, so the patron's generosity praised in love poetry rests on his people's raids.

links.note: On the road, stones stand at the forks bearing the names of undying fame (செல்லா நல்லிசைப் பெயரொடு) of warriors who gave their lives; at court the patron reflects that rich men who did not give died taking their names with them.
links.teaches: The idyll makes one argument across the road and the court: a name survives on the stone of the man who gave his life or in the fame of the man who gives his wealth, and is lost with the man who gives nothing.

source_issues: Line 407 தலையிரும்பு: tvu reads தலையிறும்பு (into the thicket), which suits the bull's flight better; our reading is kept, as flagged.
Line 481 செருவிற் சாறென follows யாறெனக் கிடந்த, which would more naturally describe தெருவின் (streets); the text may have செரு for தெரு. Marked as read.
Line 540 குன்றா நல்லிசைக் சென்றோர் has க் before ச், an irregular doubling (expected நல்லிசைச் சென்றோர்).
Line 515 prints நுகமரு ணூறை with the word boundary moved by sandhi (நுகமருள் நூறை); the karu form is copied as printed.
